opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. Looking back, 2016 was really a turning point, though at the time I didn't fully realize how big a shift it would be.

Before that, my background was much more in traditional graphics and simulation. Character animation was physics, hand-crafted controllers, and a lot of careful engineering. You'd spend months tuning parameters so a character could walk or jump naturally, and the moment you changed the environment or the body a little, everything broke. It was beautiful work, but it didn't scale.

So when I started my first data-driven animation project, the idea was simple: instead of writing all the rules by hand, could we learn them from motion capture data? We had a lot of human motion recorded, and the question was whether a model could absorb the patterns of how people move and then generate new, natural motion on its own.

What struck me first was how *different* the mindset was. In graphics, you understand every equation in your system. With learning, you hand over part of that understanding to the data and the network. Honestly, that felt uncomfortable at first. When something went wrong, you couldn't just trace it to a line of code. You had to think about the data distribution, the representation, the training process. It was a new kind of debugging, almost a new kind of intuition you had to build.

But then there were moments that were genuinely exciting. You'd see the model produce a transition between two motions that nobody had explicitly designed, and it looked natural. That gave me a strong feeling that this approach captured something real about how motion is structured, something we had struggled to write down by hand for decades.

I think that project also changed how I saw the bigger picture. Animation is about making virtual bodies move; but the deeper question is how any agent, virtual or physical, learns to act in the world. That question led me gradually from animation toward 3D vision, and then toward robotics and embodied intelligence. In a way, the 2016 project was my first step from "making things look right" to "making things learn to behave right."

So it wasn't a sudden jump into AI. It was more like realizing the tools I'd been using had limits, and that data and learning opened a door to problems I had always cared about but couldn't really solve before.

r001.rationale: The response describes learning motion patterns from motion-capture data and the unfamiliar mindset, but does not state that there was no established way to formulate data-driven animation generation as a problem when he began in 2016.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. That 2016 project really was the turning point, though at the time I didn't think of it as "moving into AI" at all. I came from the computer graphics side, where animation was all about simulation and hand-crafted models. The problem I was working on was character motion, and the traditional pipeline was painfully slow. You'd capture data, clean it, then build these elaborate rule-based systems to stitch it together, and the results still looked stiff.

What changed was that we had a large motion capture dataset sitting there and I started asking a simple question: instead of writing the rules myself, could the data tell me the rules? So we tried learning the motion directly from the data. The first experiments were honestly bad. The characters would slide, limbs would drift, and my collaborators in graphics were skeptical, because the field cared a lot about physical correctness and this approach didn't guarantee any of it.

But there was one moment I still remember. We trained a model overnight, and in the morning the character transitioned from walking to turning in a way nobody had scripted. It just emerged from the data. That was the moment I realized this wasn't a trick for one animation task. It was a different way of thinking about the problem entirely.

After that I went back and learned the machine learning fundamentals properly, which was humbling, because I was already a few years into my career. But I think coming from graphics actually helped. I had strong intuitions about what good motion looks like, and that domain knowledge turned out to be the thing that made the learning-based methods actually work in practice. So I'd say my move into AI was less a decision and more that a project pulled me in, and I just followed where it led.

r001.rationale: The response describes trying to learn character motion from a dataset, but does not say there was no established way to formulate data-driven animation generation as a problem when the project began.

sol-6.1.text: Looking back, that project was a bridge for me from animation into AI. In animation, you’re trying to create movement, and a data-driven approach changes the question: instead of specifying everything yourself, what can you learn from examples of motion? That was the shift for me—seeing data as something that could help us model movement, rather than simply something we used as a reference.
